headline: Decade-Old Flaws Expose Thousands of Servers to Remote Backdooring via Motherboard Controllers
deck: Enterprise servers from major manufacturers are vulnerable to deep, persistent access through their baseboard management controllers, posing a severe threat to corporate networks.
body: Thousands of internet-connected servers from major manufacturers can be remotely backdoored, exploiting critical vulnerabilities, some over a decade old, embedded deep within system motherboards. This poses a significant, persistent threat to corporate data centers.

These vulnerabilities reside in Baseboard Management Controllers (BMCs), miniature computers embedded into nearly every enterprise server motherboard. BMCs operate with their own operating system firmware, network stack, and unique IP address, functioning independently of the main server.

Security researchers have consistently warned since at least 2013 that BMCs, particularly through the IPMI protocol, offer a substantial gateway for hackers to gain deep, persistent access to data centers. These warnings highlighted a critical oversight in enterprise security.

Firmware security expert HD Moore recently uncovered more than a dozen new vulnerabilities within BMCs from major vendors including HPE, Supermicro, Avocent, Huawei, Lenovo, and Dell. His research, presented at the Black Hat security conference, revealed the persistent nature of these flaws.

Moore's findings are particularly troubling as they indicate that some weaknesses he identified and warned about in 2013 remain active today. This persistence occurs despite previous measures intended to fix these critical system flaws.

“The end result is a pervasive, under-monitored, under-patched parallel attack surface that is both Internet-exposed and widespread inside corporate networks, and is much more exploitable than many folks realize,” Moore wrote in an email ahead of his Black Hat presentation.

An external scan of internet-connected BMCs discovered over 86,000 devices that publicly exposed a management service. Strikingly, more than 54 percent of these internet-exposed BMCs contained at least one critical vulnerability, indicating a vast open target for attackers.

Among these exposed devices, as many as 75,000 remained vulnerable to CVE-2013-4786, a critical flaw in the IPMI 2.0 authentication protocol. This decade-old vulnerability continues to offer an entry point for sophisticated attacks.

The problem extends beyond public exposure; an internal scan of 126,761 BMCs within corporate networks found similar risks. Nearly 29 percent of these internally surveyed devices harbored one or more critical vulnerabilities, demonstrating a persistent threat even behind firewalls.

These widespread and persistent vulnerabilities in BMCs create an under-monitored attack surface that grants hackers deep access to corporate networks and data centers. Organizations face a severe, ongoing risk to their data security and operational integrity, demanding immediate and comprehensive remediation efforts.
